chicken-thigh-fried-coated-skin-coating-.title: Chicken thigh, fried, coated, skin/coating not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh is dark meat from the bird's leg. In this product the meat is first pre‑cooked, then deep‑fried in a coating. The skin and coating are not eaten and are usually removed before consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark meat contains more iron and zinc than white meat.
Deep‑frying gives the product a crispy crust and a characteristic aroma.
Chicken thighs are used in many traditional dishes, such as Japanese katsu or American fried chicken.
Pre‑cooking helps the meat stay juicy while the coating protects it from drying out.
Chicken skin is rich in collagen, but it is excluded from this serving.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: Dark meat supplies more iron and zinc than white meat, supporting immunity and metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The product contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Selenium content
items.content: Selenium in chicken meat contributes to antioxidant protection.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds saturated fat, so portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to chicken protein.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: If reused oil is used, trans fats may be present in the final product.

items.title: Salt and seasonings
items.content: Added salt during frying can be an issue for individuals with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Before eating, remove the coating and skin, then cut into pieces. The product can be served hot, added to salads, soups, or used in sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it keeps quality for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before consumption.

crackers-sandwich-reduced-fat-peanut-but.title: Crackers, sandwich, reduced fat, peanut butter filled

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑fat sandwich crackers with a peanut butter filling are a light snack consisting of two crisp whole‑grain wafers bonded by a smooth peanut butter layer. The product is low in added fats while retaining a rich nutty flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: These sandwich crackers are popular in sports nutrition because of their low calorie density and portability.
The peanut butter filling is enriched with B‑vitamins and magnesium.
Reduced fat is achieved by replacing part of the oil with air‑foaming technology during dough preparation.
The product contains no artificial colors or flavors.
Packaging is made from recyclable material, reducing environmental impact.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: The peanut butter provides about 8 g of protein per serving, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The reduced‑fat formulation makes it suitable for diets that limit fat intake.

items.title: Contains beneficial minerals
items.content: Magnesium, phosphorus and iron are present, important for energy metabolism and bone health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain wafers supply fiber that helps regular digestion.

items.title: Contains vitamin E
items.content: Peanut butter is a good source of the antioxidant vitamin E, which protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: The product contains peanut butter and can cause severe allergic reactions in individuals with peanut allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Despite the reduced fat, the snack may contain moderate salt; people monitoring sodium intake should take this into account.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While low in fat, the crackers still provide calories from carbohydrates and protein; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: These sandwich crackers are convenient as a stand‑alone snack, on hikes, or at work. They pair well with fruit, yogurt, or can be crumbled into salads for added crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place with the package tightly sealed. For longer storage (over 3 months) keep refrigerated to maintain crispness and prevent spoilage.

fish-in-lemon-butter-sauce-with-starch-i.title: Fish in Lemon-Butter Sauce with Starch, Vegetable, Frozen Meal

content.title: About
content.content: This is a ready‑to‑heat frozen meal featuring a fillet of fish coated in a fragrant lemon‑butter sauce, served with a starchy side (such as rice or mashed potatoes) and a vegetable mix. It is designed for quick reheating in a microwave or on the stovetop while preserving the fish's tenderness and the freshness of the vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lemon juice in the sauce helps keep the fish moist and adds a bright acidity.
The starchy component provides a fast source of energy and makes the dish more filling.
Typical vegetables (carrot, peas, corn) add vitamins and minerals for a balanced meal.
Frozen ready meals began mass production in the 1950s and became popular worldwide by the 1990s.
Rapid‑freeze technology is used to lock in flavor and prevent large ice crystals.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Fish, especially marine varieties, supplies EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: Vitamin C from lemon
items.content: Lemon provides vitamin C, boosting immunity and enhancing iron absorption.

items.title: Starch as a carbohydrate source
items.content: Rice or potato side quickly replenishes glycogen stores after physical activity.

items.title: Vegetables supply fiber and vitamins
items.content: Carrots, peas, and corn deliver vitamin A, vitamin K, and dietary fiber for digestive health.

items.title: Potential low‑sodium options
items.content: Choosing a low‑salt version can help maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Fish or seafood allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to fish may experience severe reactions if they consume the product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some ready‑meal formulations can be high in salt; people with hypertension should check the label.

items.title: Additive sensitivity
items.content: Preservatives and flavor enhancers may cause sensitivity in certain consumers.

items.title: Proper heating required
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave harmful bacteria; follow the manufacturer’s heating instructions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen meal in the microwave (or on the stovetop) according to the package directions, usually 3‑5 minutes. Stir well to distribute the sauce evenly and ensure the internal temperature reaches at least 75 °C. Serve immediately, optionally garnished with fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the meal frozen at –18 °C or lower. Once the package is opened, any leftovers should be transferred to an airtight container and stored in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours, then reheated thoroughly before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Gravy is a thick sauce made from meat or vegetable stock, thickened with flour, starch, or cream. It adds a rich aroma and flavor, enhancing the natural notes of vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “gravy” comes from the English term for a sauce made from meat drippings.
Traditional British gravy is made from pan juices, but many vegetarian versions use vegetable broth.
In the United States, gravy is a staple accompaniment to turkey on Thanksgiving.
There are “brown” and “white” gravies – they differ by the type of base and thickening method.
Homemade gravy can be refrigerated for up to 5 days or frozen for up to 3 months.

items.title: Improves nutrient absorption
items.content: Gravy’s small amount of fat helps the body absorb fat‑soluble vitamins from vegetables more efficiently.

items.title: Contains collagen (in meat versions)
items.content: Meat‑based stocks used in traditional gravy are rich in collagen, which supports joint and skin health.

items.title: Flavor‑rich with herbs
items.content: Herbs and spices added to the sauce can provide antioxidant benefits.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared gravies often contain a lot of salt; people with hypertension should watch portion sizes.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cream‑based versions may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate (MSG)
items.content: Some commercial gravies contain added MSG, which can cause sensitivity in certain individuals.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Serve gravy over roasted, stewed, or boiled vegetables, mashed potatoes, rice, and legumes. It can be stirred into vegetable casseroles, ragouts, or used as a base for soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared gravy in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, portion into containers and freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat to a boil before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole wheat muffin is a baked product made from whole grain wheat, offering a soft crumb and a mild nutty flavor. It works well for breakfast, a snack, or as an accompaniment to meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole wheat retains the bran and germ, making it more nutritious than refined flour.
Muffins have a relatively low glycemic index, suitable for balanced diets.
Traditional recipes often avoid added sugar, but versions may include dried fruit or nuts.
Baking with whole wheat provides more fiber than using white flour.
Muffins keep well when stored properly and stay fresh for several days.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain healthy bowel function.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole wheat supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: Helps stabilize blood sugar levels, beneficial for those at risk of diabetes.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Provides magnesium, iron, and zinc, which support muscle function and immunity.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients in whole grains protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Wheat allergy / gluten intolerance
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid whole wheat muffins.

items.title: High carbohydrate content
items.content: Overconsumption may contribute to weight gain for those monitoring calorie intake.

items.title: Added sugar in some varieties
items.content: Certain muffin recipes contain added sugars or sweetened dried fruits, increasing calories.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Muffins can be enjoyed plain, topped with butter or cheese, added to yogurt, oatmeal, smoothies, or used as a base for desserts and casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature in a cool, dry place. For longer freshness, keep them refrigerated.

content.title: About
content.content: The multigrain hot‑dog bun is a soft, slightly toasted roll made from a blend of wheat, rye, oat and whole‑grain flours. It has a mild nutty aroma and works well with both hot and cold fillings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Multigrain buns contain more dietary fiber than standard white buns.
The mix of different grains enhances flavor complexity and gives a chewier texture.
They are popular in fast‑food venues and food festivals as a “healthier” alternative.
A touch of honey or molasses is often added during baking for a subtle sweetness and golden crust.
They are commonly served with barbecue sauce or mustard.

items.title: Higher fiber content
items.content: The blend of whole grains boosts dietary fiber, supporting regular digestion.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact
items.content: Combining several flours slows the rise of blood sugar compared with pure wheat buns.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rye and oat flours provide B1, B3 and B6 vitamins important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The grain mix supplies iron, magnesium and zinc, which aid immunity and muscle function.

items.title: No trans fats
items.content: When baked correctly, the bun contains no artificial trans‑fat.

items.title: Grain allergies
items.content: People allergic to wheat, rye or oats may experience reactions.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: The bun is not suitable for gluten‑free diets.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Some versions contain added salt; individuals with hypertension should watch portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the bun lengthwise and fill with a sausage, patty, vegetables, cheese or sauces. It also works well for sandwiches with turkey, ham or vegetarian patties.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight bag at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate up to 7 days or freeze for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach is a leafy vegetable belonging to the Amaranth family. Raw spinach has a mild, slightly bitter flavor and a tender texture. It is widely used in salads, smoothies, soups, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach was known in ancient Rome and Greece, where it was used as a medicinal plant.
Its iron content is often compared to meat, but bioavailability is lower due to oxalates.
There are two main varieties: savoy (curly) and flat leaf.
Spinach is rich in chlorophyll, which gives it its bright green color.
In the 19th century, spinach became popular in the US thanks to the "Popeye the Sailor Man" advertising campaign.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in spinach converts to vitamin A, supporting vision and immunity.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Low‑calorie source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: High oxalate levels can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Raw spinach is often treated with pesticides; thorough washing before consumption is recommended.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to spinach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw spinach is perfect for salads, smoothies, wraps, and as a base for sandwiches. It can also be briefly blanched to reduce bitterness and improve nutrient absorption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store spinach in the refrigerator in an airtight container or a bag with a small amount of moisture. Use within 3–5 days. Discard if yellow spots or off‑odors appear.
